Decian Persecution
DEE-shuhn pur-suh-KYOO-shuhn
historical event
From the emperor Decius, under whom it was carried out, and persecution; the empire-wide persecution of Christians in 250–251.

Biblical Definition

The Decian Persecution was the first systematic, empire-wide persecution of the Christian church, carried out under the Roman emperor Decius in 250 and 251. Unlike earlier local outbreaks, Decius required every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice to the pagan gods and obtain a certificate proving they had done so. Christians who refused were imprisoned, tortured, and put to death; many of the church’s leaders, including bishops of Rome, Antioch, and Jerusalem, were martyred. The persecution was short but severe, and it tested the church profoundly. Many believers stood firm and won the martyr’s crown or endured imprisonment as confessors; but many others, unprepared for such fierce trial, fell away—some sacrificing outright, others purchasing certificates to feign compliance. These fallen ones, the lapsi, raised an agonizing question for the church after the persecution ended: on what terms might the lapsed be received back. The dictionary remembers the Decian Persecution as a great trial of faith that produced both glorious martyrs and grievous apostates, and that shaped the church’s understanding of repentance, restoration, and discipline. It stands as a witness that the world’s enmity against Christ is real and at times violent, that the Lord sustains His own in the fire while the unprepared and the false fall away, and that even the failures of the weak may, through genuine repentance, be met with the grace of God—a grace the church wrestled to administer rightly in the controversies that followed.

Webster 1828 Definition

The first empire-wide persecution of the church (250–251) under Decius, requiring pagan sacrifice; it produced glorious martyrs and many lapsed, raising the question of restoring the fallen.

DECIAN PERSECUTION, the first empire-wide persecution of the church, 250–251.

Under the emperor Decius, who required all to sacrifice and obtain certificates.

Christians who refused were imprisoned, tortured, and martyred.

Many bishops were killed; the church was tested profoundly.

Produced both glorious martyrs and many lapsed (the lapsi).

Key Scripture

Rev 2:10 — "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

Mat 10:28 — "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."

2Ti 3:12 — "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution."

Mat 10:33 — "But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven."

Modern Corruption

The persecution exposed the cost of discipleship and the failure of the unprepared, not a corruption of doctrine but a trial of faith.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the cost of true discipleship and the reality of the world’s enmity against Christ. The Decian Persecution tested the church as fire tests metal: those whose faith was genuine stood firm unto death or endured as confessors, while the unprepared and the false fell away. The Lord had warned that all who would live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution, and bade His own be faithful unto death for the crown of life.

The trial also exposed the danger of an unprepared and nominal Christianity. Many who had professed the faith in easier days sacrificed to idols or bought certificates of compliance when the sword was drawn, showing that not all who bear the name are truly Christ’s. Yet the persecution, by raising the question of the lapsed, also pressed the church to wrestle rightly with repentance and restoration. The dictionary holds the sober lesson: the friendship of the world is not to be expected, the faith must be counted worth dying for, and the church must be ready, in days of peace, for the days of trial that may come.

The event’s name marks the first empire-wide trial of the church, producing martyrs and the question of the lapsed.
